blocks.prompt: The Horse That Sleeps Standing Up
blocks.text: A horse sleeps standing up. Its legs can lock, so it can rest without falling over. Horses only sleep for about three hours a day. They sleep in short naps, not all at once. To dream, a horse must lie down. So a herd takes turns. Some horses lie down to dream while the others stand and watch for danger. A baby horse is called a foal. A foal can stand up about one hour after it is born. By the next day it can run with the herd.

blocks.prompt: The Horse That Sleeps on Its Feet
blocks.text: A horse can fall asleep on its feet. Inside each leg is a set of tendons and ligaments that hook together like a latch. Scientists call it the stay apparatus. When the horse locks it, the leg holds itself up. No muscles have to work. The horse can doze for hours and never wobble. But there is a catch. Light sleep can happen standing up. Deep sleep, the kind with dreams, cannot. For that, a horse has to fold its legs and lie flat on its side. A horse lying flat is slow to get up, and a slow animal is an easy meal. So horses solve the problem together. In a herd, one or two lie down and sleep deeply while the rest stand around them, ears turning, watching. Later they swap. A horse that lives alone often will not lie down at all, and after a week or two it starts to stumble from missing its dreams. All of this comes from a simple fact. A horse is not a hunter. A horse is hunted, and it is built to leave in a hurry.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: Built to Notice Everything
blocks.text: A horse has the largest eyes of any land mammal. They are not on the front of its face like yours. They sit high on the sides of the skull, and that placement changes everything. Standing still, a horse can see almost the whole circle around itself, close to 350 degrees, without moving its head. It can graze and keep watch at the same time. The price is two blind spots. A horse cannot see directly behind its tail, and, stranger still, it cannot see the ground right under its own nose. The last few inches before its mouth are hidden. To fix this, a horse uses the stiff whiskers around its muzzle to feel what its eyes cannot reach. Trim those whiskers off and you take away a sense the horse cannot replace. The ears do similar work. Each ear is moved by about ten muscles, and it can swivel almost halfway around on its own. A horse can aim one ear forward and one ear back and listen to two places at once. Other horses read those ears. In one experiment, horses chose which bucket to walk to based on where a photographed horse's ears were pointing. When the ears in the photo were covered up, the choices fell apart. None of this is decoration. Wide eyes, feeling whiskers, and swiveling ears are the equipment of an animal whose whole plan is to notice a problem early and be gone before it arrives.

answers: the eyes sit high on the sides of the skull, so it sees almost all the way around while its head is down
it cannot see the ground under its nose, so the whiskers feel what the eyes cannot reach
horses read the ear direction of another horse to decide where to go, and covering the ears broke the choice
(inference: every one of these features is a survival tool, not just an interesting detail)

5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

meta.templateLabel: The Horse That Sleeps Standing Up

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The hoof is one toe, the middle one
The horse family began about 55 million years ago
The earliest ones were the size of a small dog

blocks.prompt: Standing on One Finger
blocks.text: Look at a horse's foot and you are looking at one finger. Not a paw, not a hoof-shaped bundle of bones, but a single toe, the middle one, standing on its tip. The hoof itself is the toenail, thickened until it can carry half a ton at a gallop. The horse has been walking on tiptoe for millions of years. It did not start that way. The earliest animals in the horse family lived about 55 million years ago, and the best known of them was roughly the size of a small dog. It had four toes on each front foot and three on each back foot, and it moved through warm forest, browsing soft leaves. Spread toes work well in soft ground. They spread weight the way a snowshoe does. Then the climate dried and the forests thinned into open grassland. Out on the plains, the animals that survived were the ones that could run far and eat grass, and grass is punishing food, full of grit and silica that files teeth flat. Over millions of years, horse teeth grew taller and harder. Legs grew longer. The side toes carried less and less weight, shrank, and finally lifted off the ground entirely. Today they are still there, hidden: two thin splint bones fused along the cannon bone, the ghosts of toes two and four. Museums love to line this up in a row. Small forest creature, medium horse, large horse, each one a little taller with a little less toe, marching left to right toward the animal in the paddock. It makes a tidy poster and it is misleading. The real family tree was a thicket, not a ladder. Dozens of branches ran at the same time, some with three toes, some large, some small, most of them ending in extinction with no descendants at all. Three-toed horses and one-toed horses grazed the same plains for millions of years. The modern horse is not the goal that evolution was aiming at. It is the one branch that happened to still be standing.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Horse That Sleeps Standing Up

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The horse family evolved in North America
Gone from the Americas about 10,000 years ago
Domestic horses trace to the Volga and Don steppe
That lineage spread from about 2200 BCE
Columbus brought horses back in 1493
Przewalski's horse may be feral, not truly wild

blocks.prompt: The Horse That Came Home
blocks.text: The horse is a North American animal. That sentence surprises almost everyone, including people who live in horse country, and it is the beginning of one of the strangest round trips in the history of life. For roughly 55 million years, the horse family evolved on this continent. Nearly the whole story happened here: the small forest browsers, the drying of the climate, the shift to grass, the long legs, the loss of the side toes. North America was the workshop. Every so often, when sea levels fell and the Bering land bridge rose out of the water, some of the workshop's products walked west into Asia and kept going. That is how horses reached Europe, and later Africa, where their relatives became zebras and wild donkeys. Then, around ten thousand years ago, at the end of the last ice age, horses vanished from the Americas completely. Nobody can say for certain why. The climate was lurching, the grasslands were changing, and human hunters had recently arrived with sharp tools. Scientists still argue about how the blame should be divided, and the honest answer is that we do not know. What is certain is the outcome: for ten thousand years, the continent where the horse was invented had no horses on it at all. The animal survived in Eurasia, and there it met people. Recent genetics has sharpened the story considerably. Every ordinary riding horse alive today, from a Shetland pony to a racehorse, traces back to a single population from the steppe north of the Black and Caspian Seas. Around 2200 BCE that lineage exploded outward and replaced nearly every other horse population across Eurasia within a few centuries. That is fast. It suggests people were not just keeping horses. They were spreading a technology, and the horses that came with it were bred for something new: a calmer temperament and a stronger back. There is a wrinkle worth holding onto. For a long time, Przewalski's horse of the Mongolian steppe was called the last truly wild horse, the one line that people never touched. Then researchers sequenced ancient horse bones from a settlement in Kazakhstan and found that those managed, milked horses were not the ancestors of modern domestic horses. They were the ancestors of Przewalski's horse. On that reading, the last wild horse may be a feral one: a domesticated animal that got loose and went back to the grass. Not everyone accepts the interpretation, and the argument is live. The round trip closed in 1493, when Columbus carried horses on his second voyage across the Atlantic. Within a couple of centuries their descendants were running loose across plains their ancestors had left ten thousand years earlier. The mustangs of the American West are not a wild species returning to a wild home. They are escaped domestic animals standing in the exact landscape where the whole horse experiment began. Whether that makes them native or invasive has been argued in courtrooms, and it depends less on biology than on where you decide the story starts.

(it casts the continent as the place the horse was built and exported from; cite: North America was the workshop)
(the author refuses to pick a cause; cite: the honest answer is that we do not know; it separates what is known from what is argued)
(the replacement was too fast to be chance; cite: They were spreading a technology, plus the bred traits of calmer temperament and a stronger back)
(it reframes native versus invasive as a question about the chosen timeframe, not the animal; earned by the extinction and 1493 return evidence)
